newsitem.title: GREECE: Greek TV duel sinks in sea of voter apathy.
newsitem.headline: Greek TV duel sinks in sea of voter apathy.

text.p: A television duel between Greece's Socialist Prime Minister Costas Simitis and his conservative challenger Miltiades Evert ended in a tie, sinking in a sea of voter apathy, political analysts said on Saturday.
Both camps in the close race to next week's election had hoped Friday's much-touted TV debate, the first such clash in Greece, would tip the scales and raise voter interest.
But political commentators said the painstakingly coached candidates offered nothing new that could help wavering voters make up their minds.

"On one hand it's positive that TV will not decide the next premier in these "couch elections'," wrote Giorgos Votsis in the liberal Eleftherotypia daily. "On the other, it's a pity last night's debate only boosted voter scepticism."
Television call-in polls showed the demure Simitis and the stocky Evert were as close after the U.S.-style debate as nationwide public opinion polls put them two days ago.
Both parties claimed their candidate was best and declared victory.
The Socialists said the demure Simitis, 60, who hardly cracked a smile throughout the 90-minute clash, was serious, calm and presented his arguments well.
Conservative New Democracy party officials said the stocky Evert, 57, who repeatedly banged his fist to make a point, was energetic, direct and appeared to care for the average citizen.
"They are two leaders with different styles -- one is professorial, cool while Evert is more spontaneous," said political analyst Costas Arvanitopoulos.
With national elections only eight days away, polls show the two main parties running a close race, smaller parties gaining momentum and the Greek public remaining surprisingly apathetic.
"I didn't watch the debate, I had to work to pay my mortgage. Or are these guys going to pay it for me," an Athens taxi driver told Reuters.
An Athens area poll showed that 63 percent of those asked watched the debate. Of those, 40 percent said it helped them make up their minds and 55 percent said it did not.
Both Simitis, who called the snap election confident he was leading the polls, and Evert have opted for a media-oriented campaign rather than the traditional balcony speeches of their predecessors.
But with polls showing Greeks unimpressed by the characters and issues of the race, analysts say the modern campaign styles may have failed to inspire voters.

Past Greek elections have been dominated by flamboyant figures such as late socialist leader Andreas Papandreou and conservative party founder Constantine Karamanlis, who delighted in delivering rousing speeches before huge crowds.
Simitis, who succeeded Papandreou in January, bears little resemblance to his maverick mentor, shying away from populist rhetoric and focusing on European Union targets.
